A lightweight, modular toolkit for data access, messaging, and application infrastructure — built on standard Jakarta EE and CDI.

docs.title: What is FluDa?
docs.text:
FluDa provides a developer-friendly, fluent programming model for data access that mirrors modern APIs like Spring's JdbcClient — without the bulk of a full framework. It is organized into six standalone pillars:

  • JDBC Client

    A lightweight, type-safe, fluent query engine built directly over JDBC.

    → Getting Started jdbc-client

  • SQL Initialization

    Automates database schema management and data population on application startup.

    → Getting Started sql-init

  • Transaction Support

    Container-agnostic declarative and programmatic transaction boundaries.

    → Getting Started tx

  • Mail

    Simple mail abstraction with Jakarta Mail and pluggable providers.

    → Getting Started mail

  • Data

    A Jakarta Data implementation — @Repository interfaces with query-by-method-name, @Find, and @Query, generated at compile time and executed through JdbcClient.

    → Getting Started data

  • JMS Client

    A fluent Jakarta Messaging client with CDI wiring, payload converters and cached connections.

    → Getting Started jms-client

docs.title: Why FluDa?
docs.text:
• Lightweight

    Zero framework dependencies — built on standard CDI and Jakarta EE. No Spring, no heavyweight runtime.

  • Modular

    Use only what you need — core, config, CDI, or any combination — across every pillar.

  • Jakarta EE/CDI Friendly

    Built on standard Jakarta EE, CDI, Jakarta Data, and MicroProfile Config. Works with GlassFish, WildFly, and any compatible server.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
Add the dependency to your project:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-jdbc-core</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-Beta1</version>
</dependency>

Then create a client from any DataSource and run fluent queries:

import io.github.fludakit.jdbc.JdbcClient;

// Create a client from any DataSource
JdbcClient client = new JdbcClient(dataSource);

// Fluent queries with named parameters
List<Engineer> engineers = client.sql("SELECT id, name FROM engineers WHERE department = :dept")
        .param("dept", "Engineering")
        .query(Engineer.class)
        .list();

// Updates with generated keys
int rows = client.sql("INSERT INTO engineers (name, department) VALUES (:name, :dept)")
        .param("name", "Ada Lovelace")
        .param("dept", "Engineering")
        .update();

See the getting started guide for all options.

docs.title: Introducing FluDa: Fluent Data Toolkit for Jakarta EE
docs.text: We're excited to announce FluDa — a lightweight, modular data-access toolkit designed specifically for standard Jakarta EE and CDI environments.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: Modern Java applications often reach for Spring's JdbcClient or JdbcTemplate for fluent database access. But what if you're building on standard Jakarta EE without Spring? You're left with raw JDBC — verbose, error-prone, and lacking the developer experience that modern APIs provide.

docs.title: What FluDa offers
docs.text:
FluDa fills this gap with three standalone pillars:

  1. JDBC Client — A fluent, type-safe query engine built directly over JDBC. No framework dependencies in the core module.

  2. SQL Initialization (coming soon) — Automated schema management and data population on startup.

  3. Transaction Support (coming soon) — Declarative and programmatic transaction boundaries that work with any Jakarta EE server.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text:
The JDBC Client is available now. Check out the getting started guide to get up and running in minutes.

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-jdbc-core</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>

We'd love your feedback — head over to GitHub to explore the source, report issues, or contribute.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
FluDa (Fluent Data Toolkit for Jakarta EE/CDI) is a lightweight, modular data-access suite designed for standard Jakarta EE and CDI environments. It provides a developer-friendly, fluent programming model that mirrors modern data APIs like Spring's JdbcClient — without requiring Spring or introducing bulky dependencies.

FluDa is organized into five standalone modules:

docs.title: JDBC Client
docs.text:
A lightweight, type-safe, fluent query engine built directly over JDBC. The core module has zero framework dependencies — just JDBC and a DataSource.

  • Fluent API with named and positional parameters
  • POJO mapping with custom row mappers
  • Generated key support
  • CDI integration for dependency injection

Get started with JDBC Client →

docs.title: SQL Initialization
docs.text:
Automates database schema management and data population on application startup. Perfect for development and testing scenarios where you need to set up database state automatically.

  • Schema creation from SQL scripts
  • Data population from SQL files
  • CDI integration for automatic execution

Get started with SQL Init →

docs.title: Transaction Support
docs.text:
Container-agnostic declarative and programmatic transaction boundaries backed directly by a standard DataSource or JPA. Works in Java SE, Servlet containers, and Jakarta EE environments.

  • @Transactional interceptor for CDI beans
  • Resource-local transactions without JTA
  • Transaction propagation control
  • Transaction-phase callbacks and events

Get started with Transaction Support →

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
A simple mail abstraction with built-in Jakarta Mail (SMTP) support and pluggable providers for third-party services like SendGrid.

  • MailSender interface with JakartaMailSender implementation
  • Fluent MailBuilder for composing messages
  • Template support with FreeMarker and simple placeholder processing
  • CDI integration with MicroProfile Config properties
  • Pluggable providers — implement MailSender for any email service

Get started with Mail →

docs.title: JMS Client
docs.text:
A fluent Jakarta Messaging client in the style of Spring's JmsClient, with CDI wiring and MicroProfile Config for Java SE and Jakarta EE.

  • JmsClient with fluent send, receive, receive-selected and browse operations
  • MessageConverter SPI — SimpleMessageConverter by default, optional JSON-B
  • CachingConnectionFactory reuses one JMSContext per thread
  • CDI producers that resolve a JMSContext, a ConnectionFactory or a configured Artemis/Qpid section

Get started with JMS Client →

docs.title: FluDa Data: Jakarta Data Repositories, Generated at Compile Time
docs.text:
FluDa Data is an implementation of Jakarta Data for Jakarta EE and CDI applications. You declare a @Repository interface, and an annotation processor generates the implementation at compile time — no runtime proxies, no classpath scanning, no reflection to read your entities. The generated code renders SQL and executes it through the FluDa JDBC Client.

The project is organized into three published modules:

Module Artifact Description core fluda-data-core The runtime API: entity-model annotations (@Entity, @Identity, @AggregateRoot, @ValueObject, @Association), the generated-metadata contracts (EntityMetadata, AttributePathResolver), the SQL renderer (SqlBuilder) and its dialects, and paging/cursor support. qbn fluda-data-qbn The optional query-by-method-name parser. Add it to the annotation processor path for repositories that derive queries from method names (findBy…, countBy…, deleteBy…). processor fluda-data-processor The annotation processor. It reads each @Repository interface and emits the CDI implementation, entity metadata, reflection-free row mappers and the static metamodel.

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• @Repository — the Jakarta Data stereotype. A repository interface extends DataRepository, BasicRepository or CrudRepository with a concrete entity type, and the processor generates a matching …Impl CDI bean.
  • Compile-time generation — for every repository the processor emits the implementation plus a reflection-free EntityMetadata, a row mapper and the _Entity static metamodel. Nothing is built or proxied at runtime.
  • JdbcClient execution — generated SQL is rendered by a dialect seam (identifier quoting and pagination) and run through JdbcClient. The shipped dialects are H2 (the default) and PostgreSQL, selected with the -Afluda.dialect annotation-processing option.
  • Lifecycle annotations — @Insert, @Update, @Save and @Delete map a method signature straight to a DML statement. save/saveAll are a true upsert, as Jakarta Data defines them.
  • Finders — three ways to express a query: built-in CrudRepository methods, the Jakarta Data annotations (@Find with @By/@OrderBy, or @Query for native SQL), and query-by-method-name (findByStatus, …) via the optional qbn module.

Jakarta Data Query Language (JDQL) is not implemented

Methods annotated with @Query take native SQL supplied by your application. That SQL is not parsed or rewritten by the dialect layer, so it may be database-specific. JDQL string translation is out of scope.

docs.text:
• Start with getting started to add the processor, map an entity, declare a repository and use the lifecycle annotations, built-in methods and query-by-method-name.
  • Explore advanced topics for aggregate roots and value objects, and the roadmap for optimistic locking and domain events.

docs.title: Advanced Topics
docs.text: This page covers modeling with aggregate roots, value objects and cross-aggregate associations, and gives the current status of two planned features — optimistic locking and domain events — that are not ready yet.

docs.title: Aggregate Root
docs.text:
An aggregate is a cluster of objects that is modified as a unit through a single entry point: the aggregate root. Mark the root type with @AggregateRoot. Everything the root owns — embedded value objects, composed child entities and element collections — is persisted and loaded with it, and a save of the root cascades to the objects it owns.

import io.github.fludakit.data.annotation.AggregateRoot;
import io.github.fludakit.data.annotation.Identity;

@AggregateRoot
public class Profile {
    @Identity Long id;
    String fullName;

    Address address;                       // value object  -> flattened into this table
    List<WorkExperience> workHistory;      // entity collection -> own table, fk profile_id
    List<Education> education;             // entity collection -> own table, fk profile_id
    List<ContactPoint> contacts;           // value-object element collection -> child table
    // getters and setters ...
}

The owner's fields are classified by the type they reference:

Field Type Storage address @ValueObject Embedded — its leaves are flattened into the root's own table (address.city, address.zip, …). A value object has no identity of its own. contacts List< @ValueObject > Element collection — a child table (profile_contacts) keyed by the root's foreign key plus the flattened value-object columns. workHistory, education List< @Entity > Composition — each target is an entity with its own identity and its own table, carrying a foreign key back to the root (profile_id).

docs.title: Value objects
docs.text:
A @ValueObject is immutable in spirit and defined entirely by its attributes — it has no identity. Embedded value objects may nest (an Address may hold a GeoPoint), and their leaves are flattened into the owning table. Because they are part of the root's row, you can sort and filter through them with a dot path:

@Find
@OrderBy("address.city")
List<Profile> orderedByCity();

docs.title: Composition children
docs.text:
A composed @Entity (such as WorkExperience) manages its own table and identity, and holds a reference back to the root. The child's bare inverse field maps to the same foreign key the aggregate loader walks:

@Entity
public class WorkExperience {
    @Identity Long id;
    String company;
    int yearStart;
    int yearEnd;
    Profile profile;   // inverse reference -> profile_id
    // ...
}

Querying through a composition collection renders an EXISTS semi-join, so the root never fans out into duplicate rows and the count stays correct:

@Find
List<Profile> findByWorkHistoryCompany(@By("workHistory.company") String company);

long countByWorkHistoryCompany(String company);   // query-by-method-name equivalent

docs.title: Associations: referencing another aggregate
docs.text:
Not every relationship is composition. When a field points at an entity that belongs to a different aggregate (typically another bounded context), mark it @Association. An association is persisted as a foreign key only:

  • On write, the referenced entity's identifier is extracted into the <field>_id column; the referenced entity itself is never cascaded.
  • On read, the reference is not eagerly resolved — the field is left null and the application resolves it lazily when it needs to.
@Entity
public class Order {
    @Identity Long id;
    BigDecimal amount;
    @Association Customer customer;   // persisted as customer_id, not cascaded
    List<OrderItem> orderItems;       // composition, owned by this aggregate
    // ...
}

This keeps aggregate boundaries explicit: Order owns its orderItems, but only points at a Customer that some other aggregate owns and saves.

docs.title: Optimistic locking with @Version — not ready
docs.text:
Not implemented yet

Optimistic locking is on the roadmap but is not supported in the current version. There is no version attribute recognition, and concurrent updates are last-write-wins — a stale update is not detected or rejected. The Jakarta Data TCK's @Version suites are excluded from the conformance run for this reason.

The intended design is a version column on the entity that the generated UPDATE both increments and guards with a WHERE … AND version = :expected predicate, failing the update when the row changed underneath you. Until this lands, do not rely on a version field for concurrency control. Track progress in the issue tracker.

docs.title: Domain Events — not ready
docs.text:
Not implemented yet

Domain events are on the roadmap but there is no API for them today. Lifecycle operations do not raise events, and nothing is dispatched to the CDI container.

The intended design is to let an aggregate record domain events as its state changes (for example OrderPlaced when a new aggregate is saved) and have the generated repository publish them around the lifecycle operation, so application code can react through CDI observers instead of polling for changes. This is not part of the current release; watch the issue tracker for progress.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This guide covers adding FluDa Data to your project, mapping an entity, declaring a repository, and using the three ways to express persistence operations: the lifecycle annotations, the built-in repository methods, and query-by-method-name.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• JDK 21 or later.
  • The Jakarta Data API (jakarta.data:jakarta.data-api).
  • The FluDa JDBC Client — generated implementations execute SQL through JdbcClient. In a CDI environment add fluda-jdbc-cdi and provide a DataSource.
  • A CDI-compatible runtime to inject the generated repository beans (the processor also runs in plain builds; the generated …Impl is a CDI bean).
  • H2 or PostgreSQL. H2 is the default dialect; select PostgreSQL with -Afluda.dialect=postgresql.

docs.title: Adding dependencies
docs.text:
Add the runtime API as a normal dependency, and the processor (plus the optional query-by-method-name parser) to the annotation processor path:

<dependencies>
    <!-- Runtime API: entity-model annotations, metadata contracts, SQL rendering -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
        <artifactId>fluda-data-core</artifactId>
        <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
    </dependency>

    <!-- Jakarta Data API (@Repository, CrudRepository, @Find, @By, ...) -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>jakarta.data</groupId>
        <artifactId>jakarta.data-api</artifactId>
        <version>1.0.1</version>
    </dependency>

    <!-- Executes the generated SQL; produces JdbcClient in CDI -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
        <artifactId>fluda-jdbc-cdi</artifactId>
        <version>1.0.0-Beta1</version>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

<build>
    <plugins>
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
            <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
            <configuration>
                <annotationProcessorPaths>
                    <path>
                        <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
                        <artifactId>fluda-data-processor</artifactId>
                        <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
                    </path>
                    <!-- OPTIONAL: only needed for query-by-method-name (findBy.../countBy.../deleteBy...) -->
                    <path>
                        <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
                        <artifactId>fluda-data-qbn</artifactId>
                        <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
                    </path>
                    <path>
                        <groupId>jakarta.enterprise</groupId>
                        <artifactId>jakarta.enterprise.cdi-api</artifactId>
                        <version>4.1.0</version>
                    </path>
                </annotationProcessorPaths>
                <!-- Uncomment to target PostgreSQL instead of the default H2 dialect -->
                <!--
                <compilerArgs>
                    <arg>-Afluda.dialect=postgresql</arg>
                </compilerArgs>
                -->
            </configuration>
        </plugin>
    </plugins>
</build>

Query-by-method-name needs the qbn processor

fluda-data-qbn is an optional annotation processor dependency. A repository that derives queries from method names (findBy…, countBy…, deleteBy…) must declare it on the processor path. Without it the processor reports a compile error naming the dependency, rather than silently generating a predicate-less query.

docs.title: Mapping an entity
docs.text:
Annotate the type with @Entity and mark its identifier field with @Identity:

import io.github.fludakit.data.annotation.Entity;
import io.github.fludakit.data.annotation.Identity;

@Entity
public class Task {
    @Identity Long id;
    String title;
    Status status;

    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public void setId(Long id) { this.id = id; }
    public String getTitle() { return title; }
    public void setTitle(String title) { this.title = title; }
    public Status getStatus() { return status; }
    public void setStatus(Status status) { this.status = status; }
}

Fields map to snake-cased columns (title → title, a hypothetical dueDate → due_date) unless the type is a value object or association — see advanced topics. Enum fields round-trip through the generated mapper by name.

docs.title: Declaring a repository
docs.text:
Extend one of the Jakarta Data repository supertypes with a concrete entity and identifier type. An empty interface already gives you the full set of built-in CRUD operations:

import jakarta.data.repository.CrudRepository;
import jakarta.data.repository.Repository;

@Repository
public interface TaskRepository extends CrudRepository<Task, Long> {
}

At compile time the processor generates TaskRepositoryImpl — a CDI bean you can inject directly:

import jakarta.inject.Inject;

@ApplicationScoped
public class TaskService {

    @Inject
    TaskRepository tasks;

    public Task create(String title) {
        Task task = new Task();
        task.setTitle(title);
        task.setStatus(Status.NEW);
        return tasks.insert(task);   // returns the entity with its generated id
    }
}

docs.title: Lifecycle annotations
docs.text:
Beyond the built-in methods, you can declare your own lifecycle methods and annotate them. These are decided purely on the method signature — the method name is free:

Annotation Effect @Insert Insert a new row; fails if the row already exists. @Update Update an existing row. @Save Upsert — update, and insert if no row was updated. @Delete Delete by entity, by identifier, or by a parameter-derived predicate. 
import jakarta.data.repository.Delete;
import jakarta.data.repository.Insert;
import jakarta.data.repository.Repository;
import jakarta.data.repository.Save;

@Repository
public interface TaskRepository extends CrudRepository<Task, Long> {

    @Insert
    void store(Task task);            // name is arbitrary; the annotation decides

    @Save
    Task persist(Task task);          // upsert: insert or update

    @Delete
    int removeByStatus(Status status); // delete predicate derived from the parameter
}

Lifecycle methods accept a single entity, a List<E> or an E[], and may return void, the entity, a count, or a collection. save/saveAll follow Jakarta Data upsert semantics: an entity carrying an application-assigned identifier is inserted when the update matches no row.

docs.title: Built-in repository methods
docs.text:
Extending CrudRepository (or BasicRepository) contributes these methods, which the processor implements without any declaration on your part:

Method Purpose insert / insertAll Insert one entity, or a List/array of them. update / updateAll Update one entity, or a List/array of them. save / saveAll Upsert one entity, or a List/array of them. delete / deleteAll Delete a given entity, or a List/array of them. deleteById Delete by identifier. findById Find by identifier, returning Optional<E>. findAll Stream every entity. existsById Whether a row with the identifier exists. count The total number of entities.

The declared return type chooses the terminal operation: List/Collection/Iterable materialize a list, Set a LinkedHashSet, Stream a stream, Optional/single entity a single result, and Page/CursoredPage the paged readers.

docs.title: Query by method name
docs.text:
With fluda-data-qbn on the processor path, an unannotated method whose name is the query is analyzed at compile time. This is the counterpart to the annotation-driven methods above: the name carries the predicates, connectors, operators, ordering and limits.

@Repository
public interface TaskRepository extends CrudRepository<Task, Long> {

    List<Task> findByStatus(Status status);

    List<Task> findByStatusOrderByTitleAsc(Status status);

    List<Task> findByTitleContainingAndStatus(String text, Status status);

    long countByStatus(Status status);

    void deleteByStatus(Status status);

    List<Task> findFirst10ByStatusOrderByTitleDesc(Status status);
}

The parser honours the Jakarta Data query-by-method-name rules:

  • Connectors — And / Or, evaluated with And binding tighter than Or (SQL precedence).
  • Negation — Not, and the negated operators NotLike, NotIn, NotBetween, NotContains, NotStartsWith, NotEndsWith, NotNull.
  • Operators — Like, In, Between, GreaterThan, LessThan, GreaterThanEqual, LessThanEqual, Contains, StartsWith, EndsWith, Null, and bare equality.
  • Subject keywords — First<n> (a row limit) and Distinct.
  • Ordering — OrderBy<Property><Asc|Desc>.

A property named in a method must resolve on the entity; a name that does not is a compile error, not a silent fallback to a guessed column. Traversing a to-one relation (findByCustomerName) generates join-aware SQL.

docs.title: Annotation-driven finders
docs.text:
When the method name should not be analyzed, use the Jakarta Data annotations instead. @Find builds criteria from @By (or the parameter names when @By is absent), @OrderBy sorts, and @Query supplies native SQL:

import jakarta.data.page.CursoredPage;
import jakarta.data.page.PageRequest;
import jakarta.data.repository.By;
import jakarta.data.repository.Find;
import jakarta.data.repository.OrderBy;
import jakarta.data.repository.Query;

@Repository
public interface CustomerRepository extends CrudRepository<Customer, Long> {

    @Find
    List<Customer> findByName(@By("name") String name);

    @Find
    @OrderBy("name")
    List<Customer> findByEmail(@By("email") String email);

    @Find
    @OrderBy("id")
    CursoredPage<Customer> paged(PageRequest pageRequest);

    @Query("SELECT * FROM customer WHERE email = :email")
    Optional<Customer> byEmail(String email);
}

@Find/@Query methods are accepted exactly as declared; a relation traversal must be written in @By (for example @By("customer.name")) rather than spelled into the name.

docs.title: FluDa: Fluent Data Toolkit for Jakarta EE/CDI
docs.text:
FluDa is a lightweight, framework-agnostic JDBC client for Jakarta EE and CDI applications. It provides the fluent developer experience of Spring's JdbcClient without introducing a Spring dependency.

The project is organized into three core modules:

Module Artifact Description core fluda-jdbc-core Contains the plain JdbcClient API and helper types. It depends only on the JDK's javax.sql.DataSource. config fluda-jdbc-config Integrates with MicroProfile Config and exposes a configurable JdbcConfig bean. cdi fluda-jdbc-cdi Provides CDI producers for JdbcClient and the CDI-discovered ConverterRegistry.

The repository also includes Arquillian integration tests for GlassFish and WildFly. These examples provide a practical reference for validating Jakarta EE/CDI applications in real runtimes.

Follow this reading order:

  • Start with getting started to add the dependency, run your first query, and review configuration options such as placeholders, timeouts, and defaults.
  • Explore querying and result mapping and updates for detailed behavior.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This guide covers adding FluDa JDBC Client to your project and executing your first queries, whether in a plain Java SE application or a Jakarta EE/CDI environment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• JDK 21 or later.
  • A CDI-compatible runtime is required for the cdi and config modules, such as GlassFish 8, WildFly 41, or Weld SE.
  • The core module is usable in plain Java SE applications because it depends only on javax.sql.DataSource.

docs.title: Adding dependencies
docs.text: Choose the dependency that matches your runtime. The core module is intended for Java SE applications, while the CDI and configuration integrations are for Jakarta EE-compatible runtimes.

docs.title: Using the core JdbcClient
docs.text:
Use the following dependency when only the core fluent JdbcClient API is required:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-jdbc-core</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>

The core module has no runtime dependency beyond the JDK. It expects a DataSource supplied by the application or runtime environment.

docs.title: Integrating with CDI
docs.text:
For a CDI-managed JdbcClient, add the CDI artifact:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-jdbc-cdi</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>

This artifact depends on the core module and is intended for a CDI environment.

docs.title: Integrating with MicroProfile Config
docs.text:
The fluda-jdbc-config module is an optional addon to the CDI module that provides property-based configuration. It reads configuration properties from MicroProfile Config and produces a JdbcConfig bean, which the CDI module uses to configure the JdbcClient.

Add this dependency when you want to configure the client via properties:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-jdbc-config</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>

This module depends on the CDI module and is intended for a CDI environment with MicroProfile Config support.

All modules are published with the same version. Replace the snapshot version shown above with the release version used by your application.

docs.title: Configuration properties
docs.text:
When using the config module, the following properties can be set in META-INF/microprofile-config.properties:

Property Default Description jdbcclient.placeholder ? Placeholder used when rewriting named parameters such as :name. jdbcclient.query-timeout 0 Default query timeout in seconds. 0 means no timeout. jdbcclient.fetch-size 0 Default fetch-size hint. 0 uses the driver default.

docs.title: Placeholder rewriting
docs.text:
Named parameters are rewritten according to the configured placeholder:

Placeholder Rewritten SQL Typical database ? ? MySQL and standard JDBC $ $1, $2, ... H2/PostgreSQL : :1, :2, ... Oracle @ @name SQL Server

When jdbcclient.placeholder=$, the following SQL:

SELECT id FROM engineers WHERE id = :id AND active = :active

is rewritten before it is sent to the driver as:

SELECT id FROM engineers WHERE id = $1 AND active = $2

docs.title: In a Java SE application
docs.text:
After adding fluda-jdbc-core to your project, create a JdbcClient directly from a DataSource:

import io.github.fludakit.jdbc.JdbcClient;

import javax.sql.DataSource;

DataSource dataSource = ...; // obtain a DataSource from the application or runtime

JdbcClient client = new JdbcClient(dataSource);

The builder API also supports explicit configuration:

JdbcClient client = JdbcClient.builder(dataSource)
        .placeholder("?")
        .queryTimeout(30)
        .fetchSize(100)
        .converters(registry)
        .build();

docs.title: In a CDI environment
docs.text:
In a Jakarta EE/CDI environment, add fluda-jdbc-cdi and expose a DataSource as a CDI bean:

import javax.sql.DataSource;
import jakarta.annotation.Resource;
import jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped;
import jakarta.enterprise.inject.Produces;

@ApplicationScoped
public class DataSourceProducer {

    @Resource(lookup = "java:comp/MyDS")
    private DataSource dataSource;

    @Produces
    @ApplicationScoped
    public DataSource expose() {
        return dataSource;
    }
}

The JdbcClient is then available for injection:

import io.github.fludakit.jdbc.JdbcClient;
import jakarta.inject.Inject;

@Inject
JdbcClient client;

docs.title: Executing queries
docs.text: Once the client is available, use the fluent SQL API for both reading and writing data. The library supports both named and positional parameters in a single SQL statement.

docs.title: Named parameters
docs.text:
Use named parameters with param(...):

List<DevSummary> devs = client
        .sql("SELECT id, dev_name FROM engineers WHERE id = :id")
        .param("id", 1L)
        .query(DevSummary.class)
        .list();

docs.title: Positional parameters
docs.text:
The client also accepts positional parameters:

List<DevSummary> devs = client
        .sql("SELECT id, dev_name FROM engineers WHERE id = ?")
        .param(1L)
        .query(DevSummary.class)
        .list();

A single SQL specification cannot combine named and positional parameters.

docs.title: Overriding configuration for a query
docs.text:
The queryTimeout(...) and fetchSize(...) methods on an individual SQL specification override the client defaults for that statement.

List<DevSummary> devs = client
        .sql("SELECT id, dev_name FROM engineers")
        .fetchSize(100)
        .queryTimeout(30)
        .query(DevSummary.class)
        .list();

In practice, these defaults are useful for keeping database behavior consistent across an application while still allowing particular queries to opt into stricter or more permissive settings when needed.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: See querying and mapping for more examples of result mapping, row mappers, and streaming. Explore updates and generated keys for INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations.

docs.title: Querying and result mapping
docs.text: JdbcClient.sql(...) returns a SQL specification. It supports named parameters such as :name, positional parameters such as ?, statement hints, typed mapping, and update statements.

docs.title: Retrieving simple values
docs.text:
Use singleValue(...) or optionalValue(...) to read a single scalar result from the database.

Long count = client.sql("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM engineers")
        .singleValue(Long.class);

Optional<Long> maybeCount = client.sql("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM engineers")
        .optionalValue(Long.class);

docs.title: Mapping results to records and POJOs
docs.text:
The built-in typed mapper matches result-column labels to record components or fields. Underscores are ignored when matching a column name to a record component.

public record DevSummary(Long id, String devName) {
}

List<DevSummary> devs = client
        .sql("SELECT id, dev_name FROM engineers ORDER BY id")
        .query(DevSummary.class)
        .list();

The mapper also works with a no-argument POJO whose fields match the result columns.

The following result-access patterns are available:

  • single() requires exactly one row.
  • optional() allows zero or one row.
  • list() reads all rows before returning.
  • stream() returns a lazy stream, and the stream should be closed when work is complete so JDBC resources are released.
DevSummary one = client.sql("SELECT ... WHERE id = :id")
        .param("id", 1L)
        .query(DevSummary.class)
        .single();

Optional<DevSummary> maybeOne = client.sql("SELECT ... WHERE id = :id")
        .param("id", 1L)
        .query(DevSummary.class)
        .optional();

Stream<DevSummary> stream = client.sql("SELECT ...")
        .query(DevSummary.class)
        .stream();

docs.title: Customizing row mapping
docs.text:
Mapping can be defined inline with a lambda or reused through a dedicated RowMapper.

List<String> names = client
        .sql("SELECT dev_name FROM engineers ORDER BY id")
        .query((rs, rowNum) -> rs.getString("dev_name"))
        .list();

RowMapper<DevSummary> mapper = (rs, rowNum) ->
        new DevSummary(rs.getLong("id"), rs.getString("dev_name"));

List<DevSummary> devs = client
        .sql("SELECT id, dev_name FROM engineers")
        .query(mapper)
        .list();

docs.title: Configuring converters
docs.text:
Converters translate a database value into the Java type requested by a typed mapper or scalar query. The built-in mapper supports common conversions for numeric types, strings, booleans, SQL date/time types, and Java time types.

Use a ConverterRegistry with a standalone client:

ConverterRegistry registry = new ConverterRegistry()
        .register(UUID.class, String.class, UUID::toString)
        .register(String.class, UUID.class, UUID::fromString);

JdbcClient client = JdbcClient.builder(dataSource)
        .converters(registry)
        .build();

A converter implements Converter<S, T>:

Converter<UUID, String> converter = UUID::toString;
registry.register(UUID.class, String.class, converter);

In a CDI application, register the converter as an application-scoped bean. The CDI integration automatically discovers the generic source and target types.

@ApplicationScoped
public class UuidToStringConverter implements Converter<UUID, String> {

    @Override
    public String convert(UUID source) {
        return source.toString();
    }
}

Converters are consulted when the JDBC value is not already assignable to the requested target type.

For executing inserts, updates, and batch statements, see updates. For configuration options, see getting started.

docs.title: Updates, generated keys, and batches
docs.text: JdbcClient supports write operations, generated keys, and efficient batch updates without leaving the fluent API. The examples below cover the common patterns used when modifying data in an application.

docs.title: Updating data
docs.text:
Use update() for SQL statements such as INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE. The method returns the number of rows affected.

int rows = client
        .sql("UPDATE engineers SET dev_name = :name WHERE id = :id")
        .param("name", "Ada")
        .param("id", 1L)
        .update();

docs.title: Handling generated keys
docs.text:
When inserting a row and generated keys are required, pass a GeneratedKeyHolder to the update call.

GeneratedKeyHolder keys = new GeneratedKeyHolder();

int rows = client
        .sql("INSERT INTO engineers (dev_name) VALUES (:name)")
        .param("name", "Ada")
        .update(keys);

Object generatedKey = keys.getKey();
Map<String, Object> firstRow = keys.getKeys();
List<Map<String, Object>> allRows = keys.getKeyList();

The JDBC driver must support generated keys. getKey() returns the first column from the first generated-key row, while getKeys() and getKeyList() preserve column labels and multiple rows.

docs.title: Executing batch updates
docs.text:
Use a list of named-argument maps for batch updates:

int[] results = client
        .sql("UPDATE engineers SET active = :active WHERE id = :id")
        .batchUpdate(List.of(
                Map.of("active", true, "id", 1L),
                Map.of("active", false, "id", 2L)
        ));

For positional SQL, pass an array for each batch entry:

int[] results = client
        .sql("UPDATE engineers SET active = ? WHERE id = ?")
        .batchUpdate(new Object[][]{
                {true, 1L},
                {false, 2L}
        });

These patterns keep write operations compact and consistent while exposing the database-specific capabilities needed for generated keys and bulk updates.

For query execution, parameter binding, and result mapping, see querying and result mapping.

docs.title: FluDa JMS Client: Fluent Jakarta Messaging for Jakarta EE/CDI
docs.text:
FluDa JMS Client is a fluent, framework-agnostic client for Jakarta Messaging (JMS 3.1). It mirrors the developer experience of Spring's JmsClient — send, receive, browse, payload conversion and destination resolution — without requiring Spring or any other framework. The core module depends only on the Jakarta Messaging API; the cdi and config modules add CDI wiring and MicroProfile Config for Java SE and Jakarta EE.

The project is organized into three published modules:

Module Artifact Description core fluda-jms-core The fluent JmsClient API, the MessageConverter and DestinationResolver SPIs, CachingConnectionFactory, and the JmsConfig value type. Depends only on the JDK and the Jakarta Messaging API. config fluda-jms-config Maps fluda.jms.* MicroProfile Config properties to a JmsConfig bean, and builds Artemis or Qpid JMS connection factories from the provider sections. cdi fluda-jms-cdi Produces the CachingConnectionFactory and JmsClient beans, resolving the underlying JMSContext, ConnectionFactory or configured provider section, and applying any optional JmsConfig, MessageConverter and DestinationResolver beans.

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• JmsClient — the entry point. Build it from a ConnectionFactory in Java SE (the client creates the context) or from an existing JMSContext on Jakarta EE (the container owns it). A client is not thread-safe: it shares one JMSContext across all operations, so create one client per thread.
  • DestinationSpec — what client.destination(...) returns. It carries the send, receive and browse operations for one destination; the client is immutable, so the spec is cheap to create per call.
  • MessageConverter — turns payloads into JMS messages and back. The default SimpleMessageConverter handles String, byte[], Map and Serializable payloads; JsonbMessageConverter is an opt-in JSON-B alternative, and you can plug in your own.
  • DestinationResolver — turns a destination name into a Destination. The default SimpleDestinationResolver creates a queue per name (a topic: prefix selects a topic) and caches the result.
  • CachingConnectionFactory — a ConnectionFactory decorator that keeps one JMSContext per thread, so clients reuse a connection instead of opening one each. JmsClient never closes the context it is given; this decorator is how a Java SE application manages that lifecycle.
  • JmsConfig — an immutable bundle of credentials, session mode and default destination name, applied to a builder with config(...). The config module produces it from fluda.jms.* properties.

v1 scope

v1 covers fluent send, receive and browse over a JMSContext, payload conversion, connection caching, and CDI wiring for Java SE and Jakarta EE. Annotation-driven @JmsListener containers and a CDI event bridge are deferred to 1.1; XA transactions are out of scope.

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text:
• Start with getting started to add the dependencies and send your first message in Java SE or CDI.
  • For Jakarta EE servers, see Jakarta EE.
  • The runnable examples in fludakit/examples cover plain Java SE (jms-client-vanilla), CDI with Artemis (jms-client-artemis), AMQP 1.0 with Qpid JMS (jms-client-qpid) and Jakarta EE on GlassFish and WildFly (jms-client-jakartaee).

docs.title: Destination Resolver
docs.text: DestinationResolver turns a destination name into a Destination. The client uses it when client.destination(name) is called.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
@FunctionalInterface
public interface DestinationResolver {

    Destination resolveDestination(JMSContext context, String name);
}

docs.title: SimpleDestinationResolver (default)
docs.text:
Creates destinations on the broker through the JMSContext, caching each resolution so repeated lookups of the same name return the same destination:

  • Names prefixed with topic: resolve to a Topic
  • Everything else resolves to a Queue
client.destination("orders").send(order);          // queue "orders"
client.destination("topic:events").send(event);    // topic "events"

The cache is thread-safe (ConcurrentHashMap), so one resolver instance can be shared by clients on multiple threads.

docs.title: JndiDestinationResolver
docs.text:
Looks destination names up in JNDI — the Jakarta EE convention, where the server owns the destination definitions and the application resolves them by name.

JmsClient client = JmsClient.builder(connectionFactory)
        .destinationResolver(new JndiDestinationResolver())
        .build();

client.destination("java:comp/jms/orders").send(order);

The no-arg constructor uses a fresh InitialContext; pass a container-managed Context when the deployment requires a specific environment:

client.destinationResolver(new JndiDestinationResolver(myContext));

Lookups are not cached: the JNDI provider is expected to cache looked-up objects.

docs.title: Custom resolver
docs.text:
Implement DestinationResolver for destination resolution strategies the built-ins do not cover — for example, an explicit registry or a cloud-based destination service:

public class RegistryDestinationResolver implements DestinationResolver {

    private final Map<String, Destination> registry;

    public RegistryDestinationResolver(Map<String, Destination> registry) {
        this.registry = Map.copyOf(registry);
    }

    @Override
    public Destination resolveDestination(JMSContext context, String name) {
        Destination destination = registry.get(name);
        if (destination == null) {
            throw new JmsClientException(JmsClientException.Code.CONNECTION,
                    "Unknown destination: " + name);
        }
        return destination;
    }
}

docs.title: CDI integration
docs.text:
In a CDI environment, a single DestinationResolver bean is picked up automatically and applied to every produced client:

@ApplicationScoped
public class JmsBeans {

    @Produces
    @ApplicationScoped
    DestinationResolver destinationResolver() {
        return new JndiDestinationResolver();
    }
}

Keep one default-qualified bean per SPI — with more than one candidate the container reports the ambiguity, so qualify the extras. The bean replaces the default application-wide; for a per-client choice use the builder in plain Java SE instead.

This applies to fluda.jms.default-destination and any name passed to client.destination(name).

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This guide covers adding FluDa JMS Client to your project and exchanging your first messages in a Java SE or CDI application.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• JDK 21 or later.
  • A Jakarta Messaging 3.1 broker. The test suite and examples use Apache Artemis 2.40; any compliant provider works, and Qpid JMS 2.7 is supported for AMQP 1.0.
  • The core module is usable in plain Java SE: it depends only on the JDK and the Jakarta Messaging API.
  • The cdi and config modules need CDI 4.1 and MicroProfile Config — a CDI SE container (Weld SE with SmallRye Config) for Java SE, or a Jakarta EE 11 runtime such as GlassFish 8 or WildFly 42.

docs.title: Adding dependencies
docs.text: All modules are published under the io.github.fludakit group with the same version. Replace the snapshot version shown below with the release you use.

docs.title: Plain Java SE
docs.text:
Use the core module when you only need the fluent API and provide the connection factory yourself:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-jms-core</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>

docs.title: CDI and MicroProfile Config
docs.text:
Add the CDI module to have JmsClient produced for injection, and the config module to build the connection factory from fluda.jms.* properties:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-jms-cdi</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-jms-config</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>

cdi depends on core, and config depends on core as well — add cdi explicitly when you want the producers. The config module treats the provider clients as optional dependencies, so add the one you use:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.apache.activemq</groupId>
    <artifactId>artemis-jakarta-client</artifactId>
    <version>2.40.0</version>
</dependency>

Use org.apache.qpid:qpid-jms-client (2.7.x) instead for AMQP 1.0. On a Jakarta EE server the JMSContext comes from the container, so no provider client is needed in the application — see Jakarta EE.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Describe the broker in META-INF/microprofile-config.properties. The config module builds the connection factory from these properties — add the provider-specific module (fluda-jms-artemis or fluda-jms-qpid) to your dependencies:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-jms-artemis</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>

docs.title: Apache Artemis
docs.text:
fluda.jms.artemis.broker-url=tcp://localhost:61616
fluda.jms.artemis.username=artemis
fluda.jms.artemis.password=artemis

# Used by client.destination() - a destination name, not a Destination.
fluda.jms.default-destination=orders

docs.title: Apache Qpid JMS (AMQP 1.0)
docs.text:
Use fluda-jms-qpid instead of fluda-jms-artemis:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-jms-qpid</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>

fluda.jms.qpid.remote-uri=amqp://localhost:5672
fluda.jms.qpid.username=artemis
fluda.jms.qpid.password=artemis

fluda.jms.default-destination=orders

docs.title: Client-wide properties
docs.text: Property Default Meaning fluda.jms.username – broker username for factory-based clients; unset or blank means anonymous access fluda.jms.password – broker password for factory-based clients; unset or blank means no password fluda.jms.acknowledge-mode auto auto, client or dups-ok fluda.jms.default-destination – destination name, resolved through the DestinationResolver when client.destination() is called

docs.title: Provider sections
docs.text:
A section is active once its URL is set, and needs that provider's client on the classpath:

Property Meaning fluda.jms.artemis.broker-url Artemis core URL, e.g. tcp://localhost:61616 fluda.jms.artemis.username / .password fall back to fluda.jms.username / .password fluda.jms.qpid.remote-uri Qpid JMS URI, e.g. amqp://localhost:5672 fluda.jms.qpid.username / .password fall back to fluda.jms.username / .password

acknowledge-mode uses the same short values as Spring Boot's spring.jms.template.session.acknowledge-mode: auto (Session.AUTO_ACKNOWLEDGE, the default), client (Session.CLIENT_ACKNOWLEDGE) and dups-ok (Session.DUPS_OK_ACKNOWLEDGE). Values are matched case-insensitively and _ is accepted for -, so CLIENT and DUPS_OK both work. transacted is rejected deliberately, exactly as Spring Boot keeps it a separate flag: the fluent client never commits, so a transacted context would roll back on close — wrap an injected JMSContext in a transaction instead.

docs.title: In a Java SE application
docs.text:
Create the provider's connection factory, wrap it in a CachingConnectionFactory so the thread reuses one context, and build the client:

import io.github.fludakit.jms.CachingConnectionFactory;
import io.github.fludakit.jms.JmsClient;
import org.apache.activemq.artemis.jms.client.ActiveMQJMSConnectionFactory;

import java.io.Serializable;
import java.time.Duration;

record Order(String id, String item, int quantity) implements Serializable {
}

try (var factory = new ActiveMQJMSConnectionFactory("tcp://localhost:61616", "artemis", "artemis");
     var caching = new CachingConnectionFactory(factory)) {

    JmsClient client = JmsClient.builder(caching).build();

    client.destination("orders").send(new Order("order-1", "keyboard", 2));
}

Two things are worth noting:

  • Close the caching factory before the raw factory. JmsClient never closes the JMSContext it is given; the caching decorator owns the contexts it creates.
  • send converts the payload. The default converter sends Serializable objects as an ObjectMessage, String as a TextMessage, byte[] as a BytesMessage and a Map as a MapMessage.

Without the caching decorator, every JmsClient.builder(factory) call opens a new context — and therefore a new connection — because nothing closes it. Either wrap the factory, or create the context yourself and pass it to JmsClient.builder(context).

docs.title: Sending raw messages and message properties
docs.text:
Pass a post-processor to set properties or headers on the converted message:

client.destination("orders").send(order,
        message -> JmsMessages.setStringProperty(message, "orderId", order.id()));

When no converter fits, build the message yourself — the creator receives the client's JMSContext as the message factory:

client.destination("orders").send(context -> context.createTextMessage("manual payload"));

docs.title: Receiving messages
docs.text:
receive blocks up to the timeout and throws JmsClientException with the TIMEOUT code when no message arrives. The other variants cover the usual cases:

// one message or a timeout exception
Order order = client.destination("orders").receive(Order.class, Duration.ofSeconds(5));

// one message, or empty on timeout
Optional<Order> maybe = client.destination("orders")
        .receiveOptional(Order.class, Duration.ofMillis(500));

// one message matching a JMS selector
Order urgent = client.destination("orders")
        .receiveSelected(Order.class, "priority = 'urgent'", Duration.ofSeconds(5));

// peek at the queue without consuming: browse requires a Queue destination
List<String> ids = client.destination("orders")
        .browse(message -> JmsMessages.stringProperty(message, "orderId"));

Each receive creates a consumer, receives and closes it, so the client stays usable for further operations.

docs.title: CDI in Java SE
docs.text:
With fluda-jms-cdi and fluda-jms-config on the classpath, the connection factory, its caching decorator and the client are all produced. After configuring the broker in META-INF/microprofile-config.properties, inject JmsClient and use it:

import io.github.fludakit.jms.JmsClient;
import io.github.fludakit.jms.support.JmsMessages;
import jakarta.enterprise.context.Dependent;
import jakarta.inject.Inject;

import java.time.Duration;

@Dependent
public class OrderService {

    @Inject
    JmsClient client;

    public void place(Order order) {
        client.destination()
                .send(order, message -> JmsMessages.setStringProperty(message, "orderId", order.id()));
    }

    public Order receive(Duration timeout) {
        return client.destination().receive(Order.class, timeout);
    }
}

The produced JmsClient is @Dependent on purpose: a client is not thread-safe, so it must not be shared by concurrent callers. Inject it into a request-scoped or dependent bean, or obtain a fresh instance per operation from Instance<JmsClient>. Injecting it into an @ApplicationScoped bean pins one client — and one cached context — for the application's lifetime.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The fludakit/examples repository contains runnable modules:

Example Shows jms-client-vanilla plain Java SE, no CDI jms-client-artemis CDI + config against Artemis jms-client-qpid the same over AMQP 1.0 with Qpid JMS

Start a broker with Docker:

docker compose up -d artemis

docs.title: Jakarta EE
docs.text: In a Jakarta EE environment, nothing is configured and nothing is created in the application: the container provides a JMSContext from java:comp/DefaultJMSConnectionFactory, and the cdi module builds the client from it.

docs.title: Declaring destinations
docs.text:
Jakarta EE does not let an application create destinations at runtime. Declare the destination with @JMSDestinationDefinition and inject it:

import jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped;
import jakarta.jms.JMSDestinationDefinition;

@JMSDestinationDefinition(
        name = "java:comp/jms/orders",
        interfaceName = "jakarta.jms.Queue",
        destinationName = "orders"
)
@ApplicationScoped
public class JmsResources {
}

The annotation is repeatable — a second queue would be another annotation on the same class.

docs.title: Using the client
docs.text:
Inject JmsClient and the Queue, then pass the injected Destination rather than a name:

import jakarta.annotation.Resource;
import jakarta.enterprise.context.Dependent;
import jakarta.inject.Inject;
import jakarta.jms.Queue;

@Dependent
public class OrderService {

    @Inject
    JmsClient client;

    @Resource(lookup = "java:comp/jms/orders")
    Queue orders;

    public void place(Order order) {
        client.destination(orders).send(order);
    }
}

On a server the deployment decides the address, the queue-or-topic kind and the provider settings, while a name is resolved through JMSContext.createQueue/createTopic and ignores the resource definition. The fluda.jms.default-destination property has the same caveat — it is always a name.

Do not produce a second JMSContext bean

The server already exposes the container-managed JMSContext as a bean. A producer of your own makes the Instance<JMSContext> lookup ambiguous and deployment fails with WELD-001335: Ambiguous dependencies.

docs.title: How the CDI module resolves resources
docs.text:
JmsClientProducer uses the first of these that exists:

  1. a JMSContext bean — on Jakarta EE, the container-managed context. The client uses it as is and never closes it; credentials and session mode belong to the container.
  2. a ConnectionFactory bean — wrapped in the CachingConnectionFactory bean, so all clients on a thread share a context and a connection.
  3. a configured provider section (fluda.jms.artemis.* or fluda.jms.qpid.*) whose client is on the classpath — the config module builds the factory, wrapped the same way. Artemis is tried before Qpid when both are configured.

When none exists, production fails fast with an IllegalStateException naming the three options, rather than handing out a client that only fails on the first send.

An optional JmsConfig bean — produced by the config module from fluda.jms.* — is applied to whichever spec is used. For a factory it contributes the credentials, the acknowledge mode and the default destination; for an injected JMSContext only the default destination is applicable, and configuring credentials or a non-default acknowledge mode makes production fail loudly instead of silently ignoring them.

Optional MessageConverter and DestinationResolver beans are applied the same way, after the config: define one and every client the module produces uses it instead of the defaults. See Message Converter and Destination Resolver for details.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: The jms-client-jakartaee example runs on GlassFish 8 and WildFly 42.

docs.title: Message Converter
docs.text: MessageConverter turns payloads into JMS messages and back. The client uses it in send and receive operations.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
public interface MessageConverter {

    Message toMessage(Object payload, JMSContext context);

    Object fromMessage(Message message);

    default <T> T fromMessage(Message message, Class<T> payloadType) {
        Object payload = fromMessage(message);
        if (!payloadType.isInstance(payload)) {
            throw new JmsClientException(JmsClientException.Code.CONVERSION, ...);
        }
        return payloadType.cast(payload);
    }
}

docs.title: SimpleMessageConverter (default)
docs.text:
Handles the common payload types:

Payload JMS message String TextMessage byte[] BytesMessage Map MapMessage Serializable ObjectMessage

A payload type the converter does not know makes send fail with the CONVERSION code.

docs.title: JsonbMessageConverter (opt-in)
docs.text:
Sends payloads as JSON in the body of a TextMessage. The payload class is published in the _type message property, so a consumer that is not told the type can still rebuild it.

JmsClient client = JmsClient.builder(connectionFactory)
        .messageConverter(new JsonbMessageConverter())
        .build();

Or with a custom Jsonb instance:

Jsonb jsonb = JsonbBuilder.create(jsonbConfig);
JmsClient client = JmsClient.builder(connectionFactory)
        .messageConverter(new JsonbMessageConverter(jsonb))
        .build();

JSON-B is an optional dependency: the class loads without it, and only constructing the converter without a provider fails, with a JmsClientException naming the missing piece.

docs.title: Custom converter
docs.text:
Implement MessageConverter for payload types the built-ins do not cover:

public class AvroMessageConverter implements MessageConverter {

    private final Schema schema;
    private final DatumWriter<GenericRecord> writer;
    private final DatumReader<GenericRecord> reader;

    // ...

    @Override
    public Message toMessage(Object payload, JMSContext context) {
        GenericRecord record = (GenericRecord) payload;
        ByteArrayOutputStream out = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
        Encoder encoder = EncoderFactory.get().binaryEncoder(out, null);
        writer.write(record, encoder);
        encoder.flush();
        BytesMessage message = context.createBytesMessage();
        message.writeBytes(out.toByteArray());
        return message;
    }

    @Override
    public Object fromMessage(Message message) {
        BytesMessage bytesMessage = (BytesMessage) message;
        byte[] data = new byte[(int) bytesMessage.getBodyLength()];
        bytesMessage.readBytes(data);
        return reader.read(null, DecoderFactory.get().binaryDecoder(data, null));
    }
}

docs.title: CDI integration
docs.text:
In a CDI environment, a single MessageConverter bean is picked up automatically and applied to every produced client:

@ApplicationScoped
public class JmsBeans {

    @Produces
    @ApplicationScoped
    MessageConverter messageConverter() {
        return new JsonbMessageConverter();
    }
}

Keep one default-qualified bean per SPI — with more than one candidate the container reports the ambiguity, so qualify the extras. The bean replaces the default application-wide; for a per-client choice use the builder in plain Java SE instead.

docs.title: FluDa Mail: Lightweight Mail Abstraction for Jakarta EE/CDI
docs.text:
FluDa Mail provides a simple, framework-agnostic mail abstraction for Jakarta EE and CDI applications. It defines a clean MailSender interface with built-in Jakarta Mail (SMTP) support, and makes it straightforward to integrate third-party providers like SendGrid.

The project is organized into three core modules:

Module Artifact Description core fluda-mail-core Contains the MailSender API, MailMessage, MailBuilder, and the default JakartaMailSender implementation. Depends only on the JDK and Jakarta Mail API. config fluda-mail-config Integrates with MicroProfile Config to read fluda.mail.* properties and expose a MailConfig bean. cdi fluda-mail-cdi Provides CDI producers for MailSender and MailBuilder, wiring the core beans into a Jakarta EE environment.

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• MailSender — the core interface with a single send(MailMessage) method. The core module provides JakartaMailSender for SMTP; you can implement your own for third-party services.
  • MailMessage — a simple POJO holding from, to, subject, htmlBody, and attachments.
  • MailBuilder — a fluent builder that wraps a MailSender and optionally a TemplateProcessor for rendering email templates.
  • MailConfig — configuration POJO with SMTP/POP3 properties, produced from MicroProfile Config in the config module.

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text:
• Start with getting started to add dependencies and send your first email.
  • Explore advanced topics for custom MailSender implementations and CDI integration patterns.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This guide covers adding FluDa Mail to your project and sending your first email, whether in a plain Java SE application or a Jakarta EE/CDI environment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• JDK 21 or later.
  • A Jakarta EE 11 / CDI-compatible runtime is required for the cdi and config modules, such as GlassFish 8 or WildFly 41.
  • The core module is usable in plain Java SE applications because it depends only on the JDK and Jakarta Mail API.

docs.title: Adding dependencies
docs.text: Choose the dependency that matches your runtime. The core module is intended for Java SE applications, while the CDI and configuration integrations are for Jakarta EE-compatible runtimes.

docs.title: Using the core MailSender
docs.text:
Use the following dependency when only the core fluent MailSender API is required:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-mail-core</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>

The core module provides JakartaMailSender for SMTP. You must supply a jakarta.mail.Session configured for your mail server.

docs.title: Integrating with CDI
docs.text:
For a CDI-managed MailSender and MailBuilder, add the CDI artifact:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-mail-cdi</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>

This artifact depends on the core module and is intended for a CDI environment. The CDI module produces MailSender and MailBuilder beans, but requires either a MailConfig bean or a jakarta.mail.Session bean to be available in the container.

docs.title: Integrating with MicroProfile Config
docs.text:
The fluda-mail-config module is an optional addon to the CDI module that provides property-based configuration. It reads fluda.mail.* properties from MicroProfile Config and produces a MailConfig bean, which the CDI module uses to create a JakartaMailSender.

Add this dependency when you want to configure mail settings via properties instead of providing your own Session bean:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-mail-config</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>

This module depends on the CDI module and is intended for a CDI environment with MicroProfile Config support.

All modules are published with the same version. Replace the snapshot version shown above with the release version used by your application.

docs.title: In a Java SE application
docs.text:
In a plain Java SE application, construct a JakartaMailSender from a jakarta.mail.Session:

import io.github.fludakit.mail.JakartaMailSender;
import io.github.fludakit.mail.MailMessage;
import io.github.fludakit.mail.MailSender;

import jakarta.mail.Session;
import java.util.Properties;

// Configure your SMTP session
Properties props = new Properties();
props.put("mail.smtp.host", "smtp.example.com");
props.put("mail.smtp.port", "587");
props.put("mail.smtp.auth", "true");
props.put("mail.smtp.starttls.enable", "true");

Session session = Session.getInstance(props);
MailSender sender = new JakartaMailSender(session);

// Build and send a message
MailMessage message = new MailMessage();
message.setFrom("sender@example.com");
message.addTo("recipient@example.com");
message.setSubject("Hello from FluDa Mail");
message.setHtmlBody("<p>This is a test email sent with FluDa Mail.</p>");

sender.send(message);

docs.title: Using the fluent MailBuilder
docs.text:
The MailBuilder provides a more fluent API for constructing and sending messages:

import io.github.fludakit.mail.MailBuilder;
import io.github.fludakit.mail.JakartaMailSender;

import jakarta.mail.Session;
import java.util.Properties;

Session session = Session.getInstance(new Properties());
MailSender sender = new JakartaMailSender(session);

new MailBuilder(sender)
    .from("sender@example.com")
    .to("recipient@example.com")
    .subject("Hello from FluDa Mail")
    .htmlBody("<p>This is a test email sent with FluDa Mail.</p>")
    .send();

The builder also supports attachments:

new MailBuilder(sender)
    .from("sender@example.com")
    .to("recipient@example.com")
    .subject("Report attached")
    .htmlBody("<p>Please find the report attached.</p>")
    .attachment("report.pdf", "application/pdf", () -> new FileInputStream("report.pdf"))
    .send();

docs.title: In a CDI environment
docs.text: In a Jakarta EE/CDI environment, the fluda-mail-cdi module automatically produces a MailSender and MailBuilder bean. However, the MailSender requires either a MailConfig bean or a jakarta.mail.Session bean to be available in the CDI container.

docs.title: Using fluda-mail-config for property-based configuration
docs.text:
The fluda-mail-config module provides a MailConfig bean that is configurable via MicroProfile Config properties. Add both dependencies:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-mail-cdi</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-mail-config</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>

Then configure your SMTP settings in META-INF/microprofile-config.properties:

fluda.mail.host=smtp.example.com
fluda.mail.port=587
fluda.mail.auth-enabled=true
fluda.mail.starttls=true
fluda.mail.username=your-username
fluda.mail.password=your-password
fluda.mail.from=noreply@example.com

The config module reads these properties and produces a MailConfig bean, which the cdi module uses to create a JakartaMailSender.

docs.title: Injecting and using the mail beans
docs.text:
Once configured, inject MailSender or MailBuilder directly:

import io.github.fludakit.mail.MailBuilder;
import io.github.fludakit.mail.MailSender;
import jakarta.inject.Inject;

@ApplicationScoped
public class NotificationService {

    @Inject
    MailSender sender;

    @Inject
    MailBuilder mailBuilder;

    public void sendNotification(String to, String subject, String body) {
        mailBuilder
            .from("noreply@example.com")
            .to(to)
            .subject(subject)
            .htmlBody(body)
            .send();
    }
}

The MailBuilder is produced as @Dependent, so each injection point receives a fresh instance. The MailSender is @ApplicationScoped and backed by JakartaMailSender using the configuration from MicroProfile Config.

docs.title: Alternative: providing your own Session bean
docs.text: If you prefer to use a container-managed JavaMail session (via JNDI) instead of property-based configuration, you can produce your own Session bean. See the Jakarta EE environment section for details.

docs.title: Configuration properties
docs.text:
The following properties are supported by the config module:

Property Description Default fluda.mail.host SMTP server hostname localhost fluda.mail.port SMTP server port 25 fluda.mail.username SMTP username (empty) fluda.mail.password SMTP password (empty) fluda.mail.auth-enabled Enable SMTP authentication false fluda.mail.starttls Enable STARTTLS false fluda.mail.protocol Mail protocol (smtp or pop3) smtp fluda.mail.from Default from address (empty)

Any additional Jakarta Mail settings can be supplied through the extraProperties map on MailConfig, which is merged into the java.util.Properties passed to Session.getInstance(...). Use it for provider-specific keys that are not covered by the properties above.

docs.title: In a Jakarta EE environment
docs.text: Jakarta EE application servers (GlassFish, WildFly, Payara, etc.) provide built-in JavaMail session management via JNDI. Instead of configuring SMTP properties in microprofile-config.properties, you can use the container-managed mail session.

docs.title: Using the default mail session
docs.text:
Most Jakarta EE servers provide a default mail session at java:comp/DefaultMail. You can inject it directly and expose it as a CDI bean:

import jakarta.annotation.Resource;
import jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped;
import jakarta.enterprise.inject.Produces;
import jakarta.mail.Session;

@ApplicationScoped
public class MailSessionProducer {

    @Resource(lookup = "java:comp/DefaultMail")
    private Session defaultSession;

    @Produces
    @ApplicationScoped
    public Session mailSession() {
        return defaultSession;
    }
}

When a Session bean is available in the CDI container, the MailSenderProducer in fluda-mail-cdi automatically uses it instead of creating a session from MailConfig properties.

docs.title: Defining a custom mail session
docs.text:
You can also define a custom mail session using @MailSessionDefinition:

import jakarta.mail.MailSessionDefinition;
import jakarta.annotation.Resource;
import jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped;
import jakarta.enterprise.inject.Produces;
import jakarta.mail.Session;

@ApplicationScoped
@MailSessionDefinition(
    name = "java:comp/mail/mySession",
    host = "smtp.example.com",
    port = 587,
    from = "noreply@example.com",
    transportProtocol = "smtp",
    user = "your-username",
    password = "your-password",
    properties = {
        "mail.smtp.starttls.enable=true",
        "mail.smtp.auth=true"
    }
)
public class MailSessionProducer {

    @Resource(lookup = "java:comp/mail/mySession")
    private Session mailSession;

    @Produces
    @ApplicationScoped
    public Session session() {
        return mailSession;
    }
}

The @MailSessionDefinition annotation configures the mail session at the class level, and the container creates the corresponding JNDI resource. You then inject it via @Resource and expose it as a CDI bean.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The MailSenderProducer in fluda-mail-cdi resolves the Session in the following order:

  1. If a MailConfig bean is available (from the config module), it creates a session from those properties.
  2. Otherwise, if a Session bean exists in the CDI container (produced by your code as shown above), it uses that session.
  3. As a fallback, it creates a default session with localhost:25 and no authentication.

By exposing a JNDI-managed Session as a CDI bean, you leverage the container's mail configuration and avoid duplicating SMTP settings in your application.

See advanced topics for custom MailSender implementations and replacing the default JakartaMailSender with third-party providers.

docs.title: Mail Sender
docs.text: This page covers extending FluDa Mail with custom MailSender implementations and integrating third-party providers like SendGrid in a CDI environment.

docs.title: Creating a custom MailSender
docs.text:
The MailSender interface is intentionally minimal:

public interface MailSender {
    void send(MailMessage message) throws MailException;
}

Any email provider — SendGrid, Amazon SES, Mailgun, or a proprietary API — can be integrated by implementing this single method. The MailMessage POJO provides access to from, to, subject, htmlBody, and attachments, which is sufficient for most provider APIs.

docs.title: Example: SendGrid implementation
docs.text:
The following example shows how to wrap the SendGrid Java SDK in a MailSender implementation.

Add the SendGrid dependency to your project:

<dependency>
    <groupId>com.sendgrid</groupId>
    <artifactId>sendgrid-java</artifactId>
    <version>4.10.3</version>
</dependency>

Then implement MailSender:

import com.sendgrid.Method;
import com.sendgrid.Request;
import com.sendgrid.Response;
import com.sendgrid.SendGrid;
import com.sendgrid.helpers.mail.Mail;
import com.sendgrid.helpers.mail.objects.Content;
import com.sendgrid.helpers.mail.objects.Email;
import io.github.fludakit.mail.MailAttachment;
import io.github.fludakit.mail.MailException;
import io.github.fludakit.mail.MailMessage;
import io.github.fludakit.mail.MailSender;

import java.io.InputStream;
import java.util.Base64;

public class SendGridMailSender implements MailSender {

    private final SendGrid sendGrid;

    public SendGridMailSender(String apiKey) {
        this.sendGrid = new SendGrid(apiKey);
    }

    @Override
    public void send(MailMessage message) throws MailException {
        try {
            Email from = new Email(message.getFrom());
            Email to = new Email(message.getTo().getFirst());
            Content content = new Content("text/html", message.getHtmlBody());
            Mail mail = new Mail(from, message.getSubject(), to, content);

            // Add additional recipients
            for (int i = 1; i < message.getTo().size(); i++) {
                mail.getPersonalization().getFirst()
                    .addTo(new Email(message.getTo().get(i)));
            }

            // Add attachments
            for (MailAttachment attachment : message.getAttachments()) {
                try (InputStream is = attachment.toDataSource().getInputStream()) {
                    byte[] bytes = is.readAllBytes();
                    String base64 = Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(bytes);

                    var sdkAttachment = new com.sendgrid.helpers.mail.objects.Attachments();
                    sdkAttachment.setContent(base64);
                    sdkAttachment.setType(attachment.toDataSource().getContentType());
                    sdkAttachment.setFilename(attachment.getFilename());
                    sdkAttachment.setDisposition("attachment");

                    mail.addAttachments(sdkAttachment);
                }
            }

            Request request = new Request();
            request.setMethod(Method.POST);
            request.setEndpoint("mail/send");
            request.setBody(mail.build());

            Response response = sendGrid.api(request);
            if (response.getStatusCode() < 200 || response.getStatusCode() >= 300) {
                throw new MailException("SendGrid rejected payload: " + response.getStatusCode());
            }
        } catch (MailException e) {
            throw e;
        } catch (Exception e) {
            throw new MailException("Failed to send email via SendGrid", e);
        }
    }
}

This implementation translates the MailMessage into the SendGrid SDK's Mail object, handles Base64 encoding for attachments, and checks the HTTP response status.

docs.title: Replacing JakartaMailSender in CDI
docs.text: By default, the fluda-mail-cdi module produces a JakartaMailSender backed by a jakarta.mail.Session configured from MicroProfile Config properties. To use a different provider — such as the SendGridMailSender above — you need to supply your own MailSender bean that takes precedence.

docs.title: Option 1: CDI producer with @Priority
docs.text:
The simplest approach is to produce your own MailSender bean with a higher @Priority:

import io.github.fludakit.mail.MailSender;
import jakarta.annotation.Priority;
import jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped;
import jakarta.enterprise.inject.Produces;
import org.eclipse.microprofile.config.inject.ConfigProperty;

@ApplicationScoped
@Priority(100)
public class SendGridProducer {

    @Produces
    @ApplicationScoped
    public MailSender mailSender(
            @ConfigProperty(name = "sendgrid.api.key") String apiKey) {
        return new SendGridMailSender(apiKey);
    }
}

The @Priority(100) annotation ensures this producer takes precedence over the default MailSenderProducer in the fluda-mail-cdi module. The sendgrid.api.key property can be defined in META-INF/microprofile-config.properties or as an environment variable.

docs.title: Option 2: CDI alternative bean
docs.text:
Alternatively, mark the default producer as an alternative and provide your own:

In a CDI extension or beans.xml, you can disable the default producer. However, using @Priority is generally simpler and more maintainable.

docs.title: Using the custom sender
docs.text:
Once your producer is in place, inject MailSender or MailBuilder as usual — the CDI container resolves your custom implementation:

import io.github.fludakit.mail.MailBuilder;
import jakarta.inject.Inject;

@ApplicationScoped
public class NotificationService {

    @Inject
    MailBuilder mailBuilder;

    public void sendWelcomeEmail(String to) {
        mailBuilder
            .from("welcome@example.com")
            .to(to)
            .subject("Welcome!")
            .htmlBody("<p>Welcome to our platform.</p>")
            .send();
    }
}

No code changes are needed at the injection site. The MailBuilder produced by the CDI module depends on MailSender by type, so it automatically picks up whichever bean the container resolves — whether that is the default JakartaMailSender or your custom SendGridMailSender.

docs.title: Template Resolver
docs.text: The MailBuilder optionally integrates with a TemplateProcessor for rendering email templates.

docs.title: Template resolution in CDI
docs.text:
In a CDI environment, the MailBuilderProducer resolves the TemplateProcessor in the following order:

  1. If a TemplateProcessor bean is available in the CDI container, it uses that bean.
  2. Otherwise, it falls back to TemplateProcessor.DEFAULT, which:
  3. Checks if FreeMarker is on the classpath (via Class.forName("freemarker.template.Configuration")). If found, uses the built-in FreeMarkerTemplateProcessor.
  4. Otherwise, falls back to SimpleTemplateProcessor, a lightweight implementation that performs :name placeholder substitution.

This means you can use templates out of the box without any additional configuration — just add FreeMarker to your classpath if you want .ftl template support, or use the simple placeholder-based processor by default.

docs.title: Built-in processors
docs.text:
The core module ships with two built-in processors:

  • FreeMarkerTemplateProcessor — used automatically when FreeMarker is on the classpath. Loads .ftl templates from the classpath under templates/.
  • SimpleTemplateProcessor — a lightweight fallback that loads .subject and .body templates from the classpath and performs :name placeholder substitution.

docs.title: Using templates
docs.text:
To use templates, inject a TemplateProcessor bean or rely on the default:

new MailBuilder(sender, templateProcessor)
    .from("noreply@example.com")
    .to("user@example.com")
    .locale(Locale.FRENCH)
    .template("welcome", Map.of("name", "Alice"))
    .send();
